lesson.title: How Squishy Is an Electron Cloud
lesson.summary: Polarizability is the ease with which an atom or molecule's electron cloud can be distorted into a temporary dipole, and it is the property that determines how strong London dispersion forces will be.
lesson.body:
Polarizability measures how easily the electron cloud surrounding an atom or molecule can be pushed out of its normal, even distribution by an external influence, whether that influence is a nearby ion, a polar molecule, or just the fleeting instantaneous dipole of a neighboring atom. A highly polarizable electron cloud distorts readily, forming a larger induced dipole in response to a given nudge, while a less polarizable electron cloud resists distortion and forms only a small induced dipole under the same conditions. Since London dispersion forces are built entirely from these induced, temporary dipoles, polarizability is the direct physical property that determines how strong dispersion forces will be between any two atoms or molecules.

The electrons responsible for this effect are, appropriately, the outer valence electrons, and two structural factors control how tightly or loosely those electrons are held. The first is simply the total number of electrons, since molecules or atoms with more electrons generally have larger, more diffuse electron clouds that are easier to distort. The second, closely related factor is atomic or molecular size and volume; even at a fixed number of electrons, a molecule with more physical volume spreads its electron density over a larger space, and electrons farther from the nucleus are held less tightly, since the nucleus's positive charge has to act over a greater distance, making the outer electrons more responsive to outside distortion.

The halogen group offers a clean illustration once again. Moving down the group from F2 to Cl2 to Br2 to I2, both the number of electrons and the overall size of the molecule increase steadily. Iodine's outer electrons are held far more loosely than fluorine's, since they sit much farther from the nucleus and experience more shielding from inner electron shells, making I2 considerably more polarizable than F2. This greater polarizability produces stronger London dispersion forces in I2, which is the direct explanation for why I2 is a solid at room temperature while F2 is a gas, even though both are nonpolar diatomic molecules with the identical, symmetric linear geometry.

Polarizability also explains apparent exceptions to simple mass based predictions of boiling point. Comparing molecules of similar molar mass but different shapes shows that a more elongated, easily distorted molecular shape typically has higher polarizability, and therefore a higher boiling point, than a more compact, spherical shape of the same mass, because the compact shape holds its electrons more symmetrically and offers less surface area for close contact with neighboring molecules. This size and shape dependent view of polarizability is what ultimately justifies the earlier claim that London dispersion forces, while often ranked as the weakest intermolecular force, can become the dominant force in large, highly polarizable molecules, sometimes producing higher boiling points than smaller molecules that rely on dipole-dipole forces or even hydrogen bonding.
